chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, who said:

I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: The sick person must give the adhān and iqāmah when he intends salat, even within himself if he is unable to speak them. He was asked: And if he is in severe pain? He said: There is no alternative but that he give the adhān and iqāmah, because there is no salat except with adhān and iqāmah.
So the correct understanding of this report is the emphasis of recommendation and encouragement toward the greatness of the reward in it, not that what is intended by it is obligation.

key_terms.الثَّوَابِ: reward granted for performing the act
key_terms.الْمَرِيضِ: the sick person who is the subject of the ruling
key_terms.شَدِيدَ الْوَجَعِ: being in severe pain or intense illness
key_terms.يُؤَذِّنَ: to pronounce the adhān before salat
key_terms.يُقِيمَ: to pronounce the iqāmah before salat

ai.seo_question: Does a sick person have to recite the adhān and iqāmah before salat in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith states that even a sick person should perform the adhān and iqāmah before salat, at least inwardly if unable to utter them aloud. The concluding clarification explains that this wording indicates strong recommendation and encouragement due to its great reward, not legal obligation.
